name: Effort justification
statement: People who suffer or work hard to get something are said to rate it more highly afterwards, because the effort would otherwise look wasted.
meaning: Aronson and Mills took the prediction from Festinger's dissonance theory, which is entry 24. Someone who has paid an unpleasant price for membership holds two thoughts that do not sit together: the price was steep, and the group is dull. The price cannot be unpaid, so the group improves. Two features of the claim get lost in retelling. It is about the person who did the work, not about anyone watching. And it revalues the thing the effort bought, not the effort itself.

origin.where: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
origin.note: The paper is titled "The effect of severity of initiation on liking for a group" and ran at 59(2), 177-181. It cites one work, Festinger's 1957 book, and calls the prediction a consequence of dissonance theory rather than a new idea. The name effort justification is not used anywhere in it. Aronson and Mills call the claim the hypothesis that an unpleasant initiation raises liking, and later writers, including Lodewijkx and Syroit, label it the severity-attraction hypothesis.

evidence: Sixty-three college women were told they were joining an ongoing discussion group on the psychology of sex, 21 to each of three conditions. Thirty-three volunteered and 30 were recruited later from a psychology course, and the two samples were pooled. Women in the severe condition read twelve obscene words and two vivid passages of sexual writing aloud to a male experimenter as an admission test. Women in the mild condition read five words related to sex but not obscene, among them prostitute and virgin. Controls read nothing. One woman declined the test and one guessed the procedure, and both were excluded. All three groups then heard the same tape, built to be as dull as the authors could manage, of three women discussing secondary sex behaviour in lower animals. They rated the discussion and the members on 17 scales running from 0 to 15, fourteen written and three answered aloud. Summed, the control group averaged 166.7, the mild group 171.1 and the severe group 195.3. Severe beat control at t = 3.32, p < .01, and mild at t = 2.33, p < .05, on two-tailed tests. Control and mild did not differ, t = 0.49. The gap sat mostly in the nine scales about the discussion, 97.6 against 80.2 in the control group, t = 3.66, p < .001, rather than the eight about the participants, 97.7 against 89.9, t = 2.03, p < .05.

replication.headline: Two later attempts to raise liking by making entry unpleasant found no difference, and the one modern paper to test the mechanism head on found the effect without the dissonance.
replication.detail: Lodewijkx and Syroit pooled two of their own field studies of Dutch student organisations, one with a severe initiation and one with a mild one. The severe organisation supplied 202 newcomers, from which two random subsamples of 46 were drawn, and the mild one supplied 46, for 138 in three groups. The severity manipulation held: newcomers rated their experiences 4.03 and 4.28 in the two severe subsamples against 3.56 in the mild one, F(2, 77) = 9.17, p < .001, on five-point scales. Group attractiveness did not follow, F(2, 111) = 1.41, p < .25. Attractiveness rose over the initiation in every condition alike, from 3.90 to 4.09, F(1, 111) = 18.30, p < .001. Rated severity did not correlate with attractiveness at either point, r(94) = -.09, p = .37, and r(94) = -.06, p = .58. What did predict attractiveness was companionship among newcomers, R2 = .081, p < .01, and depressive mood, which predicted it downwards, r(94) = -.53, p < .001. Kamau put 70 participants through a severe or mild admission with about half then rewarded. Her abstract reports that severe initiation did not raise group identity above mild, that reward did, that mild initiation with a reward beat severe initiation with a reward, and that effects on ratings of the discussion were not significant. Campbell, Wang and Inzlicht ran six studies with 2,883 participants on whether effort raises how meaningful a task feels. It did, up to a point. Their Study 5 tested the dissonance account directly by paying some participants a 50% bonus, which should supply the justification dissonance says is missing. It made no difference to the pattern. Of 802 recruited, 690 were analysed, and the harder task felt more meaningful, F(1, 686) = 14.33, p < .001, partial eta squared = 0.02. Higher pay slightly raised rated meaning rather than lowering it, F(1, 686) = 5.02, p = .025, partial eta squared = 0.007, and the two did not interact. The authors report no evidence that post-hoc effort justification produced the effect.

study.cite: Lodewijkx, H. F. M., & Syroit, J. E. M. M. (2001). Affiliation during naturalistic severe and mild initiations: Some further evidence against the severity-attraction hypothesis. Current Research in Social Psychology, 6(7), 90-107.

limits: The 1959 paper reports no effect size and no confidence interval, so the structured fields on this page are empty rather than filled with arithmetic done here. It gives means and standard deviations and nothing more. Its evidence is 63 women in one laboratory, and the severe advantage on the eight scales about the group members reached only p < .10 against the mild condition. The paper also contradicts itself on how the scales split. Its results text says eight scales on the discussion and seven on the participants, while its method and its Table 1 say nine and eight. The figures on this page come from Table 1, which sums to 17. Gerard and Mathewson published a replication using electric shocks in 1966, in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology at 2(3), 278-287. Elsevier returns 403 to automated requests for it, Crossref holds no abstract, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy, so it was not read. What it found appears here only as Harmon-Jones describes it. Schopler and Bateson's 1962 paper in the Journal of Personality sits behind a Cloudflare challenge at Wiley, with no open copy in Unpaywall or OpenAlex. Lodewijkx and Syroit and Alessandri and colleagues describe it the same way, and both descriptions are used as theirs. Kamau was read in abstract only, at Europe PMC. Her repository record at Birkbeck holds the published file but restricts it to repository staff, which is not the journal paywall. Aronson published a single-author follow-up on effort and the attractiveness of stimuli in 1961, at 63(2), 375-380 of the same journal. That citation comes from Crossref, the paper is closed in Unpaywall, and it was not read, so nothing is claimed about it. No preregistered direct replication of Aronson and Mills was located on 21 September 2026, in a search covering Crossref, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, OSF and web search. The 2024 multilab dissonance replication tested induced compliance, not initiation, and entry 24 carries it. The field study is correlational in the ways field studies are. The two Dutch organisations differ in size, politics, group composition and length of initiation as well as in severity, and its authors say so.
misreadings: The most common substitution is the IKEA effect, entry 49. That effect is about people valuing objects they assembled, and Norton, Mochon and Ariely separate it from this one on the grounds that Aronson and Mills admitted every participant, so whether the effort succeeded was never varied. Sunk cost is a third thing, entry 1: it concerns whether to keep spending, not how the outcome is rated afterwards. The second misreading is that the field evidence vindicates hazing. Lodewijkx and Syroit found initiations raising attraction whatever their severity, and traced that rise to newcomers spending time together rather than to what was done to them. The third is scale. One study of 63 women, whose largest reported contrast is 195.3 against 166.7 on a summed 17-item scale, is the whole of the original demonstration. The fourth is that the mechanism is settled. Alessandri, Darcheville and Zentall got the effect in 42 French children aged 7 and 8, with no group and no social judgement. Each child clicked a rectangle seven times, then met two shapes either at once or after an 8-second delay. On test trials the children preferred the rewarded shape that had followed the delay, 62.3%, t(41) = 2.76, p < .01, Cohen's d = .86. The matching preference among the unrewarded shapes was 55.5% and did not beat chance, t(41) = 1.50, p = .14. The authors argue that contrast between a bad prior event and the outcome is a more parsimonious account than dissonance. Harmon-Jones answers that contrast should work whether or not the effort buys the reward, and reads Gerard and Mathewson as showing it does not. On his account their shocked participants rated the group lower, not higher, when told the shocks were unrelated to joining. Zentall replied in 2017 under the title "Cognitive dissonance or contrast? It could be both". The dispute is open and this page does not settle it.

Retried on 21 September 2026: Elsevier returns 403 to automated requests, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy. Not read.

Retried on 21 September 2026: Wiley serves a Cloudflare challenge, and no open copy is listed. Its result appears here only as Lodewijkx and Syroit and Alessandri and colleagues describe it.

Paywalled at the journal, and the Birkbeck repository record holds the file but restricts it to repository staff. The result is taken from the abstract at Europe PMC.
